name: Methotrexate for alopecia
lead: Methotrexate is an antimetabolite immunosuppressant used in several skin and rheumatic diseases that has been prescribed off-label for severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks hair follicles, either alone or alongside corticosteroids [1][2][16]. The appearance case is direct for the people it is aimed at: in responders, the goal is regrowth of scalp and body hair lost in patches or, in severe forms, across the whole scalp or body.

Alopecia areata affects roughly 0.1 to 0.2 percent of people at any time, with a lifetime risk of about 1 to 2 percent, and the hair loss is associated with distress, anxiety and depression in some patients [16]. A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis described a paucity of definitive evidence and guidelines for methotrexate in this setting, and its pooled evidence comes from retrospective observational studies [1]. Newer JAK inhibitors, which are approved for severe alopecia areata, are now being compared head to head with methotrexate in registered trials [5][16].
infobox: Oral (also injected or applied in some reports)

paras: Dermatologists use methotrexate for alopecia areata that is extensive or has not responded to local treatments such as corticosteroid injections, typically in a specialist setting with laboratory monitoring [1][2]. It has also been reported in combination with pulse corticosteroids to improve response and limit steroid exposure [3][7]. Wikipedia lists it among options alongside corticosteroids, minoxidil, topical immunotherapy and JAK inhibitors, noting that no treatment works for everyone and that spontaneous remission complicates judging any therapy [16].

Methotrexate interferes with folate-dependent metabolism and dampens the activity of rapidly dividing immune cells. Because alopecia areata involves T-cell attack on hair follicles and a breakdown of their normal immune privilege, immunosuppression is the rationale for its use [16]. It is a long-established drug; a letter in The Lancet in 1973 on methotrexate and alopecia is an early reference in the literature [8].

The 2019 meta-analysis in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology examined methotrexate as monotherapy and as an adjunct to corticosteroids. As summarized in its abstract, methotrexate was reasonably effective in severe alopecia areata, adults responded better than children, combination treatment gave a higher complete response rate than methotrexate alone, many patients relapsed when treatment was tapered, and complication rates were acceptable. The authors noted that included studies were retrospective with variable protocols and that data beyond one year for adjunctive treatment were scarce [1].

A Brazilian retrospective, uncontrolled study of 31 patients reported more than 50 percent regrowth in about 68 percent. Response was higher with methotrexate plus corticosteroids (77.3 percent) than methotrexate alone (44.4 percent), and was highest in patients with shorter disease duration, men, adults over 40 and multifocal disease. No serious adverse effects were reported and about a third of responders relapsed [2].

A French real-life evaluation looked at pulse corticosteroid plus methotrexate, and a later French single-centre cohort followed long-term patient-reported perceptions of methylprednisolone pulses with or without methotrexate [3][7]. A report of three cases described individual patients [4].

Methotrexate is a systemic immunosuppressant requiring monitoring, according to the studies cited above [1][2]. One report documented elevated transaminases after sessions in which methotrexate was delivered into the scalp by a drug-delivery technique, raising questions about systemic absorption; the report prompted published comment and a reply from the authors [9][10][11]. The Brazilian series reported no serious adverse effects [2].

Registered trials include a Phase 3 study of methotrexate in severe alopecia areata (NCT02037191, n=90, started 2014), a comparison with triamcinolone acetonide in recalcitrant disease, a pediatric comparison with cyclosporine, a microneedling combination, a topical methotrexate versus minoxidil trial, and a Phase 4 tofacitinib versus methotrexate trial in 78 patients [5][6][12][13][14][15].

Published evidence is summarized above: a systematic review of retrospective studies, case series, a French cohort and case reports [1][2][3][4][7]. No large randomized, placebo-controlled trial results are cited here.

Per Wikipedia, triamcinolone injections were associated with over 50 percent regrowth in 80.9 percent of patients in a 2020 systematic review, and 5 percent topical minoxidil was more than eight times as likely as placebo to produce over 50 percent regrowth at six months in a 2019 review. The FDA authorized baricitinib for severe alopecia areata in June 2022, ritlecitinib (Litfulo) in June 2023 and deuruxolitinib (Leqselvi) in July 2024 [16].

card.summary: Old immunosuppressant tried off-label for alopecia areata, supported by small studies and a meta-analysis.
card.note: Systemic immunosuppressant requiring medical monitoring; reports of raised liver enzymes with scalp delivery.

quick.overview:
Methotrexate is an immunosuppressant sometimes prescribed off-label for alopecia areata, alone or with corticosteroids.

A 2019 meta-analysis noted limited definitive evidence; most data come from small or retrospective studies. Newer JAK inhibitors are now compared against it in trials.
quick.mechanism: It suppresses immune activity, which is thought to be relevant because alopecia areata is autoimmune.
quick.risks: It is a systemic prescription drug; a report found raised liver enzymes after scalp delivery sessions. Requires medical supervision.

Regrowth of scalp or body hair
angle.text: For people with severe alopecia areata, methotrexate is prescribed to quiet the autoimmune process that causes patchy hair loss. Retrospective studies report regrowth in a portion of patients, higher with corticosteroids, with relapse reported after tapering.
